summary:
This evaluation covers 12 evals (95 iterations total, no run failures). Five evals ("neg-bedrock", "neg-agentcore", "neg-access-denied", "neg-weather", "neg-ec2-resize") were negative-trigger tests (should_trigger: false); all passed trigger checks (5/5) for both variants, but expected_output, assertions, metrics, and consistency were marked skipped for these since they don't apply — these should be read as absent data, not as weaknesses for either variant.

Across the remaining 7 "content" evals, a very consistent pattern emerges: with_skill met the expected output and passed assertions at or near 100% in six of the seven evals (sagemaker-sec-verify-vs-prescribe, sm02-mixed, owns-vs-defers, read-only, encryption-rule, schema-shape), while without_skill scored 0% on expected_output and had very low assertion pass rates (0-13%) in those same six evals. In many of the specific per-assertion breakdowns, the pattern is "with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails" repeatedly, meaning this is a broad, consistent gap rather than an isolated assertion issue.

One notable exception is "sagemaker-sec-read-only," where without_skill actually passed 100% of its assertions (2/2) despite its expected_output pass_rate showing 0/5 — this discrepancy suggests the expected_output judgment and assertion-level judgment disagreed for that eval, and the small assertion count (2) limits confidence in that read.

The first eval, "sagemaker-sec-assessment," is more mixed: with_skill passed 6/7 assertions (86%) and 1/5 on expected_output, while without_skill passed only 1/21 assertions (5%) and 0/5 on expected_output. One assertion ("calls only read-only operations...") failed for both variants (an "always_fails" pattern), indicating that specific behavior needs work regardless of variant. Another assertion was flagged "flaky" for without_skill, and without_skill's output_consistency here was rated "inconsistent" (score 1.67), while with_skill's consistency wasn't scored (null) in this eval.

Where output_consistency was measured, with_skill tended to score "consistent" or "mostly_consistent" (scores 2.33–3.0) across evals where data existed; without_skill's consistency was scored in only two evals (one "mostly_consistent" at 2.67, matching with_skill exactly, and one "inconsistent" at 1.67), with consistency data null/absent for without_skill in most other evals — so consistency comparisons rest on sparse data for without_skill.

On runtime and cost, with_skill consistently took longer and cost more (e.g., 2m34s/$1.29 vs 1m43s/$0.86 in sagemaker-sec-assessment; 7-11s/$0.06-0.10 vs 0-6s/$0.00-0.06 in the shorter evals). In several evals without_skill's runtime rounds to 0s and cost to $0.00, which combined with its near-zero expected_output and assertion pass rates raises the possibility that without_skill produced little or no substantive output in those runs rather than a genuinely fast/cheap high-quality response — this is a pattern worth independent verification rather than a confirmed finding.

The quality comparison dimension (pairwise LLM-judged quality) was skipped for all 7 content evals (0 pairs evaluated, 5 skipped each), so no direct head-to-head quality judgment is available anywhere in this dataset; the content differences described above come entirely from expected_output and assertion-level pass rates, not from the quality comparison mechanism.

In sum: across content-generating evals, with_skill showed substantially higher expected_output and assertion pass rates and somewhat more consistent outputs, while taking longer and costing more; without_skill was faster/cheaper (sometimes negligibly so) but failed the large majority of expected_output and assertion checks in six of seven content evals, with one eval (read-only) showing an internal inconsistency between expected_output and assertion results for without_skill worth double-checking. One assertion type (read-only-operations claim) failed for both variants, pointing to a shared gap rather than a variant-specific one. The five negative-trigger evals show both variants correctly avoiding firing when they shouldn't, with no other dimension available for comparison there.

sagemaker-sec-assessment.summary:
This single chat-task eval looked at a SageMaker security/prevention assessment scenario, comparing without_skill and with_skill across trigger behavior, expected-output match, assertions, cost/runtime, quality comparison, and consistency.

Trigger: The behavior under test fired in 4/5 runs (80%), measured once across the pair rather than per-variant, so this is a shared precondition rather than a differentiator.

Expected output: Both variants struggled to meet the expected output overall — without_skill passed 0/5 (0%) and with_skill passed 1/5 (20%). Confidence in with_skill's judgment was high and in without_skill's was medium, so neither result should be read as strongly validated, but the direction (with_skill slightly ahead) is based on reasonably solid evidence.

Assertions: Here the gap is much larger — with_skill passed 6/7 (86%) vs without_skill's 1/21 (5%). Note the denominators differ (7 vs 21 assertion-instances), reflecting different numbers of underlying runs/samples. Looking at the per-assertion breakdown:
- Five distinct assertions (classification of Verifiability, N/A vs Passed for unreadable controls, SM-NN check ID formatting, read-only framing of the assessment, N/A reporting when no resources exist) show a clear "with_skill passes, without_skill fails" pattern, each with high-confidence judgments on the passing side (though without_skill's failures include some low-confidence judgments, meaning those specific failure calls are less certain).
- One assertion (SageMaker check IDs with severity/status) is flaky for without_skill (1/3 pass) while with_skill passes its single instance — not a clean split.
- One assertion (stating the response only calls read-only Describe/List/Get operations) fails for both variants (with_skill 0/1, without_skill 0/3) — this indicates a shared gap or an assertion/behavior that neither variant satisfies, not a point of difference.

Metrics: without_skill ran faster (1m43s vs 2m34s, ~51s less) and cheaper ($0.86 vs $1.29), with slightly lower context utilization (4.5% vs 6.3%). These efficiency advantages for without_skill stand in contrast to its much lower pass rates on expected output and assertions — a tradeoff between speed/cost and apparent correctness on this task, not an automatic win for either side.

Quality comparison: No quality pairs could be evaluated (0 evaluated, 5 skipped), so there is no direct quality-preference signal available here — this dimension is simply absent data.

Consistency: without_skill's outputs were rated "inconsistent" across repeated runs (score 1.67, with 2 "mostly consistent" and 1 "inconsistent" dimension outcomes, high confidence), suggesting its answers varied run to run. with_skill has no consistency data recorded (null), so no comparison can be made on this dimension — it's missing for with_skill rather than being a strength.

Overall: The strongest and most confidently-measured signal is in the assertions, where with_skill passed nearly all distinct checks and without_skill failed most, with one assertion flaky and one failing for both. Expected-output pass rates were low for both, slightly higher for with_skill, under medium-to-high confidence. without_skill was notably faster, cheaper, and showed signs of run-to-run inconsistency; with_skill's consistency and quality-comparison data are simply unavailable. No single dimension here should be treated as a final verdict; the picture is a tradeoff between without_skill's efficiency and with_skill's higher assertion/expected-output pass rates, with several data gaps (quality pairs, with_skill consistency, shared trigger measurement) limiting how far the comparison can be pushed.

sagemaker-sec-verify-vs-prescribe.summary:
This eval covered a chat task about explaining AWS Config/SageMaker rule classifications (Verifiable, Heuristic, Prescribe-only) and the N/A status behavior. The triggering behavior under test fired in all 5 runs (5/5), so the scenario was reliably exercised for both variants.

On expected output, there is a stark and consistent split: with_skill met the expected output in all 5 runs (5/5, 100%, high confidence), while without_skill met it in none of its runs (0/5, 0%, high confidence). This is corroborated at the assertion level — with_skill passed all 25 individual assertions (100%), while without_skill failed all 20 assertions it was evaluated on (0%). Notably, every one of the 5 distinct assertion types (covering mentions of Verifiable, Heuristic, and Prescribe-only classifications, references to N/A status, and the explanation that Prescribe-only checks are always N/A and never Passed/Failed) shows the identical pattern: with_skill passes fully, without_skill fails fully. There is no assertion that both variants pass or both fail — the split is uniform across every measured criterion, and all judgments carry high confidence, so this isn't a weak or noisy signal.

Quality comparison data is absent: all 5 pairs were skipped and none were evaluated head-to-head, so no direct quality judgment can be drawn from that dimension — this is missing data, not a tie or a weakness.

On efficiency, without_skill was notably faster (2s vs 7s average runtime) and cheaper ($0.02 vs $0.06 average cost), with slightly lower context window utilization (3.8% vs 4.5%). Ordinarily such efficiency differences would be a tradeoff worth weighing against output quality, but here without_skill's speed/cost advantage coincides with it failing to meet the expected output and all assertions, so the efficiency gain comes alongside a substantive correctness gap rather than being a neutral tradeoff.

Output consistency (how stable each variant's responses were across repeated runs) was essentially identical between the two: both variants scored "mostly_consistent" with the same overall score (2.67) and the same dimension-count breakdown (2 consistent, 1 mostly consistent), both at high confidence. So neither variant showed more run-to-run variability than the other.

In sum: the two variants are indistinguishable on response consistency, show no comparable quality-judgment data, and differ on runtime/cost (without_skill cheaper and faster) and on expected-output/assertion success (with_skill passing uniformly, without_skill failing uniformly) — the latter being a substantial and consistently measured gap across every assertion type in this eval.

sagemaker-sec-sm02-mixed.summary:
Both variants reliably triggered the behavior under test (5/5), so the scenario itself fired as expected in all runs for both.

From there, the two variants diverge sharply. with_skill met the expected output in all 5 runs (5/5, high confidence) and passed every per-assertion check (25/25, 100%). without_skill failed to meet the expected output in any run (0/5, high confidence) and passed only 2 of 15 assertion checks (13%).

Looking at the individual assertions (each evaluated across without_skill's 3 available runs, with_skill's 5):
- "Identifies the stale SageMaker access aspect as Prescribe-only (blocked Generate* verb)": with_skill 5/5, without_skill 0/3 — a clear pass/fail split.
- "Mentions the IAM Identity Center aspect": with_skill 5/5, without_skill 0/3 — clear split.
- "Mentions the blocked Generate* verb": with_skill 5/5, without_skill 0/3 — clear split.
- "Classifies the aspects as Prescribe-only": with_skill 5/5, without_skill 2/3 — without_skill passed this one most of the time, flagged as flaky (inconsistent across without_skill's own runs).
- "States the IAM Identity Center config aspect is N/A because it's not readable from the control plane": with_skill 5/5, without_skill 0/3 — clear split.

So on every assertion, with_skill passed consistently, while without_skill passed only partially on one assertion and failed the rest entirely. These confidence levels are reported as high, so the measurement itself appears reliable rather than a borderline/low-confidence judgment call.

On cost and runtime, with_skill took ~8s and cost ~$0.07 per run, while without_skill registered ~0s runtime and $0.00 cost — suggesting without_skill may not have performed the expected work at all (consistent with its 0/5 expected-output result and widespread assertion failures), rather than being a genuinely faster/cheaper execution. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (with_skill 4.5%, without_skill 3.6%), with no compaction events for either.

No quality comparison data is available: all 5 pairs were skipped, so there's no side-by-side quality judgment to weigh. Output consistency (run-to-run stability) is also not available for either variant (null), except for the one flaky assertion noted above for without_skill.

Overall, this is a one-sided result on the measured dimensions: with_skill met expectations and passed assertions consistently, while without_skill did not meet the expected output in any run and failed nearly all assertions, with its near-zero runtime/cost hinting it may not have engaged with the task the way intended. However, no quality-comparison or consistency data exists to add further nuance, and this is a single eval of five runs — a limited sample for drawing broad conclusions.

sagemaker-sec-owns-vs-defers.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task (AWS Prevention / SageMaker AI security domain), run 5 times per variant. The triggering behavior under test fired reliably in all runs (5/5), confirming the test scenario itself was exercised correctly.

The clearest and most consequential finding is a large gap in meeting the expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 5 runs (100%, with high-confidence judgments and no low-confidence flags), while without_skill met the expected output in 0 of 5 runs (0%, also judged with high confidence, so this is not a measurement artifact of weak confidence). This pattern repeats consistently across all three per-assertion checks that were scored: explaining that specific-denial diagnosis is deferred to a separate skill (and that this skill reports static posture only), citing Security Hub control IDs SageMaker.1–5 as cross-references, and stating that Security Hub is cross-referenced rather than directly called. In each case with_skill passed every run (5/5) and without_skill failed every run (0/4, with one run apparently not evaluated for assertions). Aggregated assertion pass rates reflect the same story: with_skill 15/15 (100%) vs without_skill 0/12 (0%). There is no assertion in this eval that both variants pass or both fail — all three distinguish the variants in the same direction, which strengthens the signal rather than being an artifact of one unusual assertion.

Runtime was essentially identical (6s for both), and cost was very close ($0.05 for with_skill vs $0.06 for without_skill) — not a meaningful differentiator here. Context window utilization was low for both (4.5% vs 3.7%), with no compaction events for either.

Direct quality-comparison pairs could not be evaluated at all (0 of 5 pairs scored, 5 skipped), so no quality-favorability signal is available from that dimension — this is a gap in the data, not a tie or a loss for either variant.

Output consistency differed modestly: with_skill was rated fully "consistent" (score 3.0 across all three dimensions), while without_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.0 across all three dimensions), both with high-confidence judgments. This suggests without_skill's outputs varied somewhat more run-to-run, though both remained in generally stable territory.

Overall, the dominant signal in this dataset is the expected-output and assertion pass-rate gap, which is large, consistent across all scored assertions, and backed by high-confidence judgments — not a borderline or low-confidence result. Runtime, cost, and context usage are essentially comparable between variants, and the quality-comparison dimension provides no usable data. Consistency slightly favors with_skill as well, reinforcing rather than conflicting with the expected-output finding.
</summary>

sagemaker-sec-read-only.summary:
Both variants reliably triggered the behavior under test (5/5), so the test condition itself fired consistently for both.

The clearest divergence is on "expected output": with_skill met the expected output in all 5 runs (high confidence, no low-confidence judgments), while without_skill met it in 0 of 5 runs. This is a notable and consistently-measured gap, not a borderline call.

However, the per-assertion data complicates a simple "without_skill failed" reading. Only 2 assertion checks were defined, and both were run against a much smaller sample for without_skill (1 run each) versus with_skill (5 runs each) — and both assertions passed 100% for both variants wherever they were evaluated. These two assertions are therefore not discriminating between the variants; they passed universally and don't explain or corroborate the 0/5 expected-output failure for without_skill. This suggests either the expected-output check is capturing something the assertions don't test, or the assertion sample for without_skill is too thin (only 2 total checks vs 10 for with_skill) to draw a confident conclusion about where without_skill's output diverges.

Quality comparison data is absent: all 5 pairs were skipped, so there's no direct quality judgment to weigh against the expected-output gap. Output consistency was only measured for with_skill ("mostly_consistent", high confidence); without_skill has no consistency data at all, so we can't tell whether its outputs vary run-to-run.

On efficiency, without_skill ran faster (~3s vs ~9s) and cheaper (~$0.03 vs ~$0.08), with slightly lower context-window utilization (3.7% vs 4.5%); neither showed any context compaction.

Overall: the main finding is a large, high-confidence gap in meeting expected output (with_skill 5/5, without_skill 0/5), but this isn't corroborated by assertion-level data (which is too sparse for without_skill and uniformly passing for both), isn't accompanied by any quality-comparison evidence (all skipped), and isn't offset against consistency data for without_skill (missing). Variant_a is faster and cheaper to run. Given the missing quality and consistency data for without_skill and the thin assertion sample, the expected-output result should be weighed as a real but not fully contextualized signal rather than a complete picture of output quality.

Confidence in these judgments is reported as high (not low), so this is not a weak signal.

Overall, this is a case where nearly every measurable dimension (expected output, all assertions) points the same direction with high confidence, while cost/runtime and quality-comparison data are either uninformative (likely artifacts of incomplete output) or unavailable (skipped quality pairs, missing consistency data for without_skill).

Per-assertion detail: this pattern is consistent across all 6 underlying assertions (covering the Check_ID pattern format "SM-##", naming the Verifiability field, and listing the Passed/Failed/N/A status values). In every single assertion, with_skill passed all its runs (5/5 or equivalent) and without_skill failed all of its runs (0/1 each). There is no assertion where both variants pass, none where both fail, and none where without_skill outperforms with_skill — the failure pattern is uniform across all checks, not concentrated in one specific requirement. Overall assertion pass rate: with_skill 30/30 (100%), without_skill 0/6 (0%).

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged ~11s and ~$0.10 per run; without_skill averaged ~1s and ~$0.01 per run — without_skill was substantially faster and cheaper. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.5% vs 3.7%), with no compaction events for either.

Overall state: there is a stark, consistently-measured gap in task success — with_skill met the expected output and passed all assertions every time, while without_skill failed the expected output and every assertion every time, across all 5 runs. This is offset by without_skill being much faster and cheaper to run, but given it did not meet the expected output in any run, the speed/cost advantage comes alongside a complete lack of successful task completion in this eval. Quality and consistency data for without_skill are unavailable (skipped/null), limiting how fully the tradeoff can be characterized beyond the pass/fail results.
